food.text: By about 1800 BCE, Native Americans of the eastern woodlands were cultivating several food plants. The first four known to be domesticated at the Riverton Site in Illinois were goosefoot, sunflower, marsh elder and squash. This began a slow shift from hunting and gathering toward farming.

Maize from Mexico reached the Eastern Woodlands around 200 BCE. At first it was grown as a supplement to local crops, but as its yields increased it gradually came to dominate. Eventually the older local crops were thoroughly replaced by maize-based farming.

On the Pacific Northwest Coast, salmon runs, shellfish, herring, halibut, sea mammals, berries and roots supported unusually dense settlement for hunter-gatherers. This food wealth made large villages and extensive trade possible.
food.source_title: Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast

food.text: In the Three Sisters method, maize and beans are planted together in mounds, with squash planted between them. The cornstalk holds up the climbing beans, the beans add nitrogen to the soil, and the squash leaves shade the ground to keep it moist and hold back weeds.

The squash first grown in the Eastern Woodlands was raised for its edible seeds and to make small containers from the gourds, not for the thick flesh of modern squash. Domestication in the region may not have happened until about 1000 BCE.

The most important plant in the diet of Northwest Native Americans was the camas bulb, a member of the asparagus family. People managed it by clearing land, tilling, weeding and planting bulbs. Individuals or kin-groups were recognized as the stewards of particular camas plots.
food.source_title: Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast

food.text: Hohokam farmers acquired cotton, tepary beans, sieva and jack beans, cushaw and warty squash, and southwestern pigweed between 300 and 500 CE. These plants presumably came through trade with peoples in the area of modern Mexico.

Maize spread slowly northward because its seeds and growing know-how had to cross inhospitable deserts and mountains. It also does not flower under the long summer days north of tropical Mexico, so it needed genetic adaptation. Farmers had to develop more productive varieties to suit cooler climates and shorter growing seasons.

By about 500 BCE, seeds from six domesticated plants were an important part of the diet of Native Americans in the middle Mississippi River valley. Farming there rested on local plants long before maize became dominant.
Celilo Falls on the Columbia River was used as a fishing site and trading hub by many Indigenous peoples. It is described as the longest continuously inhabited site in the Americas.
food.source_title: Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast

art.text: The Adena people carved small stone tablets with graceful stylized animal shapes or curving geometric designs in deep relief. Paint found on some suggests they were probably used to stamp designs on cloth, animal hides, or even their own bodies. They may also have been used to outline designs for tattooing.

The Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks in Ohio are eight monumental earthworks built between about 1 and 400 CE. They form large geometric shapes covering several acres and reflect precontact science, astronomy and sacred architecture. UNESCO inscribed them as a World Heritage Site on September 19, 2023.

Ancestral Puebloans excelled at rock art, including carved petroglyphs and painted pictographs. Their Barrier Canyon Style pictographs were placed where the images were shielded from the sun yet visible to the public. Many of the designs include human-like forms.

Hopewell sites in Ohio hold exotic goods from across North America, including obsidian from Wyoming, shells from the Gulf of Mexico and copper from Michigan's upper peninsula. These materials were fashioned into elaborate artifacts such as carved sheets of mica and stone animal effigy pipes.

The Adena Mound near Chillicothe, Ohio, is the type site for the Adena culture. Carbon dating places its construction between 100 BCE and 40 CE, and it stood 26 feet tall before its 1901 excavation. Inside was the Adena Pipe, later designated Ohio's state artifact.

Radiocarbon dating in 2014 determined that the Great Serpent Mound in Ohio was built in 300 BCE by the Adena peoples, and a 2019 study corroborated this. The mound is 1,348 feet long and is the largest serpent effigy known in the world. Archaeologist Brad Lepper later challenged the attribution to the Adena.

The so-called Holy Ghost panel in Horseshoe Canyon is considered one of the earliest uses of graphical perspective. Its largest figure appears to take on a three-dimensional representation. It is a Barrier Canyon Style work attributed to Ancestral Puebloans.

Adena pottery was thick, tempered with grit or crushed limestone, and mostly plain, cord-marked or fabric-marked. One type bore a nested-diamond design incised into its surface. Unlike other artifacts, Adena pottery was not buried with the dead or with the remains of the cremated.

Hopewell traders exchanged finished goods such as steatite platform pipes far and wide. Examples have been found among grave goods in many burials outside the Midwest. The Hopewell exchange system ran from the northern shores of Lake Ontario south to the Crystal River Indian Mounds in Florida.

Brad Lepper argued that the Adena are not known to have built effigy mounds or used serpent symbolism in their art. He noted that the Fort Ancient culture built the Alligator Effigy Mound in Granville, Ohio, and frequently depicted serpents. He concluded that Fort Ancient people likely built Serpent Mound.

The Toolesboro site in Iowa is a group of seven burial mounds on a bluff above the Iowa River, built between 100 BCE and 200 CE. Mound 2, the largest remaining, is 100 feet in diameter and 8 feet high. It was possibly the largest Hopewell mound in Iowa.

The Hopewell exchange system ran from the northern shores of Lake Ontario to the Crystal River Indian Mounds in Florida. Major manufacturing areas converted raw materials into products and exported them, and finished goods such as steatite platform pipes have been found in burials far outside the Midwest.

science.text: At Newark, the Octagon Earthworks were built by the Hopewell culture between 100 BCE and 400 CE. Scholars have demonstrated that they form a lunar observatory for tracking the Moon's orbit during its 18.6-year cycle.

The Octagon Earthworks at Newark, Ohio, were built by the Hopewell culture between 100 BCE and 400 CE. Scholars have demonstrated that they form a lunar observatory for tracking the Moon's orbit through its 18.6-year cycle.

At High Bank Works in Ohio, a large circle and an octagon, each roughly 1,000 feet across, line up with the sun's path on both solstices. They also line up with the moon's path during the lunar standstill cycle, suggesting the Hopewell people had advanced knowledge of astronomy.

Eight monumental Hopewell earthworks in Ohio were built between approximately 1 and 400 CE. Their large geometric shapes cover several acres each, and they are described as showing the richness of precontact culture, science, astronomy and sacred architecture.

The Octagon Earthworks combine an Observatory Mound, a 20-acre Observatory Circle and a 50-acre Octagon. The Octagon has eight walls, each 550 feet long and 5 to 6 feet high, joined to the Observatory Circle by parallel walls.

The Newark Earthworks were built between 100 BCE and 400 CE and once covered about 3,000 acres. The complex contains the largest earthen enclosures in the world, and the Octagon's primary purpose is believed to have been scientific.

politics.text: Around 300 CE, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent in Teotihuacan was desecrated, and construction in the city turned in a more egalitarian direction. Builders focused on comfortable stone accommodations for the population. Some authors see this as a sign of changing political organization.

At its height, perhaps between 1 CE and 500 CE, Teotihuacan was the largest city in the Americas. Its population likely sat around 100,000, and 80 to 90 percent of the valley's people lived there. The city is thought to have been established around 100 BCE.

The Hopewell tradition was not a single culture or society but a widely dispersed set of populations connected by a common network of trade routes. From 100 BCE to 500 CE, the exchange system ran from the northern shores of Lake Ontario south to the Crystal River Indian Mounds in Florida.

Between 250 and 350 CE, political power at Teotihuacan shifted from the Temple of the Feathered Serpent and its surrounding palace to the Avenue of the Dead Complex. Some authors believe this represents a move from a centralized, monarchical system to a more decentralized and bureaucratic organization.

Archaeologists have proposed that the Ancestral Puebloans emerged around the 12th century BCE. They had a complex network linking hundreds of communities and population centers across the Colorado Plateau. The kiva, a congregational space used mostly for ceremonies, was an integral part of their community structure.

The Hopewell interaction sphere encompassed much of North America, from the Rocky Mountains to Florida, with southern Ohio at its center. Exotic goods such as obsidian from Wyoming, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, and copper from Michigan's upper peninsula have been found in huge quantities at Ohio sites.

The Adena culture existed from 500 BC to 100 AD, centered on modern Ohio. It was probably a number of related societies sharing a burial complex and ceremonial system. It is seen as the precursor to the Hopewell tradition, which is sometimes thought of as an elaboration of Adena traditions.

During Teotihuacan's Period II, from 1 CE to 350 CE, explosive growth made it the largest metropolis in Mesoamerica. Volcanic eruptions destroyed other settlements, and newcomers poured in. The influx led to a reorganization of housing into the multi-family compounds that typify the city.

The Point Peninsula complex in present-day Ontario and New York is thought to have been influenced by the Hopewell traditions of the Ohio River valley. This influence seems to have ended about 250 CE, after which burial ceremonialism was no longer practiced.

philosophy.text: Hopewell earthworks in Ohio are described as depicting the richness and depth of precontact culture, science, astronomy, and sacred monumental architecture. Built between approximately 1 and 400 CE, eight of them were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on September 19, 2023.

Ancestral Puebloans held a distinct knowledge of celestial sciences that found form in their architecture. The kiva, a congregational space used mostly for ceremonies, was an integral part of their community structure.

Adena societies shared a burial complex and ceremonial system, and began mound building ceremonialism at the end of the Archaic period. The Adena are seen as the precursor to the Hopewell tradition, which is sometimes thought of as the zenith of Adena traditions.

The Great Serpent Mound in Ohio is the largest serpent effigy known in the world, 1,348 feet long. Radiocarbon dating in 2014 determined that the Adena peoples built it in 300 BCE, a date corroborated in 2019.

The Newark Earthworks were used as places of ceremony, social gathering, trade, worship, and honoring the dead. The complex contains the largest earthen enclosures in the world and once covered about 3,000 acres.

culture.text: In southern Ohio, the Hopewell built monumental earthworks of large geometric shapes between approximately 1 and 400 CE. Eight of these sites are now preserved as the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks. UNESCO inscribed them as a World Heritage Site on September 19, 2023.

The Adena culture, which existed from 500 BC to 100 AD, built mounds as part of burial rituals. Mortuary buildings were meant to keep and maintain the dead until their final burial. Before the earthwork was raised, utilitarian and grave goods were placed on the floor of the structure, which was then burned with the goods and the honored dead inside. Earth was piled atop the burned building, and a new mortuary building was often placed on the new mound. After several repetitions of this cycle, a prominent earthwork remained.

The Basketmaker culture of the Southwest was named for the large number of baskets found at its archaeological sites. Basketmakers wore sandals of woven yucca fibers, and hides or blankets of yucca fibers and rabbit fur were likely used for warmth. Women may have worn aprons on special occasions.

Exotic goods from across North America reached the Ohio Hopewell sites in huge quantities. These included obsidian from Wyoming, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, and copper from Michigan's upper peninsula. They were fashioned into artifacts like carved sheets of mica and stone animal effigy pipes.

Newark Earthworks in Ohio was built by the Hopewell culture between 100 BCE and 400 CE and contains the largest earthen enclosures in the world. Its Octagon Earthworks comprise a lunar observatory for tracking the Moon's orbit during its 18.6-year cycle. The whole complex once covered about 3,000 acres.

The Marksville culture of the lower Mississippi valley, active from 100 BCE to 400 CE, buried people of high social status in mounds. Their graves held imported exotic goods such as copper panpipes, earspools, mica figurines, freshwater pearls and stone platform pipes. Leaders organized community life and officiated at burial ceremonies.

At Mound City in Ohio, the Hopewell built a group of 23 earthen mounds, each covering the remains of a charnel house. The Hopewell people cremated their dead, then burned the charnel house itself and raised a mound over the remains. They also placed artifacts such as copper figures, mica, projectile points, shells and pipes in the mounds.

Marksville burial ceremonies may have been held years apart. Those who died between ceremonies were temporarily stored in other locations, and their remains were later gathered up and buried together. The mounds themselves were built in stages over many years, beginning with a flat, low platform.

At Hopeton Earthworks in Chillicothe, Ohio, the Hopewell built a circle 320 metres across and a similarly sized square. The circle has the same diameter as those at four other geometric Hopewell sites. A pair of parallel earthen lines there follows the sun's path on the winter solstice.

Marksville pottery was often decorated with geometric and effigy designs, usually stylized birds. This decorated ware was made primarily for ceremonial use, while plainer pottery served daily needs. Its similarity to pottery from Illinois and Ohio suggests larger interaction networks than had been presupposed.
